lesson.title: Conditioning and reinforcement

lead.text: In the 1890s the Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs when he noticed that they began to drool before any food reached them, at the sight of the person who usually brought it. He turned that observation into an experiment. Food makes a hungry dog drool without any training, and a bell makes it prick up its ears and do little else.

Pavlov rang the bell just before the food arrived, again and again. After enough of these pairings the dog drooled at the bell alone. The bell had become a conditioned stimulus, a signal that has gained its power through experience, and drooling at it was learned. Learning in which a signal comes to predict an outcome through repeated pairing is called classical conditioning.

The pairing matters. A bell that rings at random times, with no link to the food, teaches the dog nothing, because the bell tells it nothing about what comes next. That leaves a question about pace. The first pairing is the biggest surprise to the dog and later ones surprise it less, and a simple rule describes how the learning grows.

In 1972 Robert Rescorla and Allan Wagner proposed that rule. Call the strength of the link between bell and food V, the associative strength. It starts at 0 and can rise towards a maximum, written λ (the Greek letter lambda), which is the most the food can support. With food present, λ = 1.

Each pairing closes a share of the gap between V and λ. The rule is ΔV = rate × (λ − V), where ΔV is the change in V on that trial and the rate says how quickly the animal learns, a number between 0 and 1. Take a rate of 0.25. On the first pairing V is 0, so the gap is 1 and V rises by 0.25 × 1 = 0.25. On the second pairing the gap is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, so V rises by 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.1875 and reaches 0.4375. The figure shows six pairings.

afterFigure.text: Each step is smaller than the one before, because less of the gap is left to close. The first pairing teaches the most and the tenth teaches very little. That fits the dog that is quick to start drooling and then settles into a steady response.

lead.text: A bell is paired with food twice. The rate is 0.3, the maximum is 1, and V starts at 0.

Suppose the bell keeps ringing after the food has been taken away. The same rule applies, with one change. With no food the most the bell can predict is 0, so λ = 0. If V stands at 0.8 and the rate is 0.25, the gap λ − V is −0.8, which is negative, so V moves down by 0.25 × 0.8 = 0.2 to 0.6. A bell that no longer predicts food loses its power, trial by trial. This fading response is called extinction.

Extinction does not wipe the dog's learning clean. If the bell is rung again after a rest, the drooling often returns for a while, which is called spontaneous recovery. It looks as though extinction adds a second piece of learning, that the bell no longer means food, on top of the first and leaves the first in place. The simple rule treats extinction as unlearning, so it is a good first model and an incomplete one.

steps.headline: A bell has V = 0.5. Find V after one trial with the bell alone, at a rate of 0.2.

workedSteps.text: With no food, the maximum λ is 0.

lead.text: Now the rate is 0.5 and the maximum is 1 with food. The bell is paired with food twice, then presented alone once. When the bell is alone, the maximum is 0.

The dog has so far learned from what comes before an event: the bell. Now ask what happens to an action that is followed by something. Teach the dog to sit by giving it a treat each time it sits, and it sits more often. Sitting was followed by a consequence, and the consequence changed how likely the behaviour is. This is operant conditioning, studied by B. F. Skinner and, before him, by Edward Thorndike.

Two choices describe any consequence. It either adds something or takes something away, and psychologists call these positive and negative, words that only mean added and removed. It also either makes the behaviour more likely, which is reinforcement, or less likely, which is punishment.

The treat for sitting adds something pleasant and sitting rises, so it is positive reinforcement. A car's seat-belt alarm stops once the belt is fastened, so removing an unpleasant sound makes fastening more likely, which is negative reinforcement. A library fine takes money away and late returns fall, which is negative punishment. Touching a hot hob adds pain and the touching falls, which is positive punishment.
Decide whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell.

A trainer must also decide how often to give the treat. The rule for when a reward is given is a schedule of reinforcement. Some schedules depend on how many responses the animal makes, and some depend on how much time has passed.

A fixed-ratio schedule gives a reward after a set number of responses, such as every fourth peck. Under a variable-ratio schedule the number changes unpredictably around an average, so the reward might follow 2 pecks, then 7, then 3. A fixed-interval schedule rewards the first response after a set time has passed, so the reward lands on a response and responses during the wait earn nothing. A variable-interval schedule makes the wait unpredictable. The figure records responses over time for a fixed ratio of 4 and a variable ratio that averages 4.

afterFigure.text: The two pay out about equally often, but they differ in what happens when the rewards stop. On a fixed schedule the animal soon sees that the pattern has broken and gives up. On a variable-ratio schedule it cannot tell a long gap from the end of the rewards, so it keeps responding for far longer. An angler whose fish bite after an unpredictable number of casts knows the effect.

lead.text: A pigeon pecks a key on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule: every fifth peck is rewarded.
A rat is on a fixed-interval schedule with a wait of 10 seconds. Only a press can earn the reward.

lesson.orientation: Track how a signal gains associative strength and how reinforcement schedules shape behaviour.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A dog hears a bell just before it is fed, every time. After a few days it starts to drool at the bell alone.

Nobody taught the dog to drool at a bell. Drooling at food is automatic, and the bell was a sound the dog had no reason to care about. Something in hearing the bell and then eating changed what the bell means to the dog. That is learning, and it happened without any effort from the dog.

This lesson follows one animal through three kinds of training. First it learns what a signal predicts, and the lesson works out how fast that learning grows and what happens when the prediction stops coming true. Then it learns what its own actions earn, a different kind of learning with its own vocabulary. Last, the lesson looks at how often rewards should arrive, since the pattern of rewards shapes behaviour as strongly as the rewards do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll track how a signal gains strength with each pairing, and name the consequence or schedule behind a behaviour.

recap.keyIdea: Learning from pairings closes a share of the remaining gap each time, so gains shrink. Consequences and reward schedules then shape behaviour, and unpredictable schedules resist extinction best.

blocks.text: You found that two pairings at a rate of 0.3 give V = 0.51, and that a bell alone then pulls V back towards zero. Thirty pecks on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule earned 6 rewards, and a fixed 10-second interval allowed only 5.

recap.nextHook: Behaviour follows what it earns. Judgement can go wrong in a quieter way, as when an airport scanner beeps at a bag and you must decide how worried to be, and the next lesson starts there.

questions.prompt: A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of plays, averaging one win in twenty. Which reinforcement schedule is this?
hints: Decide whether rewards depend on time or on the number of responses, and whether that number is predictable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Variable ratio: rewards follow an unpredictable number of responses.

questions.onCorrect: Rewards after an unpredictable number of responses form a variable-ratio schedule, the hardest to extinguish.

misconceptions.feedback: Fixed means the same number every time. This payout is unpredictable.
An interval depends on time. This payout depends on the number of plays.

questions.prompt: A child's screen time is taken away after they hit a sibling, and the hitting becomes less frequent. Which consequence is this?
hints: Ask whether something was added or removed, and whether the behaviour rose or fell.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Something pleasant is removed (negative) and the behaviour decreases (punishment).

questions.onCorrect: Something pleasant was removed and the behaviour fell: that is negative punishment.

misconceptions.feedback: Positive punishment adds something unpleasant. Here something pleasant was taken away.
Negative reinforcement makes the behaviour more likely. Here it became less frequent.
Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant and the behaviour rises. Here it fell.

questions.prompt: The rate is 0.6, the maximum is 1 and V starts at 0. What is V after two pairings?
hints: Work one trial at a time.
The first trial adds 0.6 × (1 − 0).
On trial two the remaining gap is 1 − 0.6.
questions.onCorrect: Each step closes the same share of what is left: 0.6, then 0.24 more.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the first step twice. The second step is smaller because less gap is left.
That multiplies by V, not by the gap. The gap is the maximum minus V.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of bell and food teaches the dog the most?
hints: Think about how much is left to learn by each pairing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first: it starts from nothing, so there is the most left to learn.

questions.onCorrect: Learning is fastest at the start, when the most is left to learn. You reasoned out the shape of the learning curve.

misconceptions.feedback: Think about how much is left to learn by the fifth pairing.
Think about how much is left to learn by the tenth pairing.

questions.prompt: The rate is 0.5, the maximum is 1 and V starts at 0. What is V after one pairing?
hints: ΔV = rate × (λ − V).
Here λ − V is 1 − 0.
Multiply the rate by the gap.
questions.onCorrect: One pairing adds the rate times the whole gap, since V starts at zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats one pairing as learning everything. Each pairing closes only a share of the gap.
That multiplies the rate by itself. Multiply it by the gap instead.

questions.prompt: What is V after two pairings?
hints: Work one trial at a time.
The first trial adds 0.3 × (1 − 0).
On trial two the remaining gap is 1 − 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: The second step closes the same share of a smaller gap, so V grows more slowly the more it has.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the first step twice. The second step is smaller because less gap is left.
That is the value after only the first pairing.

questions.prompt: Why does V fall on a bell-alone trial?
hints: What does the bell now predict?

acceptedIdeas: With no food, the maximum is 0, so the gap is negative.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Without food the bell predicts nothing, so the maximum is 0 and the change is negative.

choices.label: The bell wears out with use.
With no food, the maximum is 0, so the gap is negative.
The dog forgets as time passes.

questions.onCorrect: No food means λ is 0. The gap is then negative, so V moves down.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule has no wear-out term. The change comes from the gap.
Time does not appear in the rule. The change comes from the gap.

questions.prompt: Starting from V = 0, what is the final V?
hints: Compute the two pairings first.
On the bell-alone trial the target is 0.
Move V halfway towards 0 from its value after two pairings.
questions.onCorrect: On the bell-alone trial V moves a share of the way towards 0: unlearning that is partial, not total.

misconceptions.feedback: That is V before the bell-alone trial. The final trial changes it.
That wipes out all learning. The rule moves V only part of the way to the target.

questions.prompt: Praise follows a pupil raising a hand, and hand-raising becomes more frequent. Is this positive or negative reinforcement?
hints: Was something added or removed, and did the behaviour rise or fall?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Positive reinforcement: praise is added and the behaviour rises.

questions.onCorrect: Something was added and the behaviour rose, so it is positive reinforcement.

misconceptions.feedback: Negative means something is removed. Was anything removed here?
Punishment makes the behaviour less likely. Here it became more frequent.

questions.prompt: A pigeon on a fixed-ratio 5 schedule makes 30 pecks. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: Fixed ratio 5 means a fixed number of responses per reward.
Count how many complete sets of five fit in 30.
Divide 30 by 5.
questions.onCorrect: Every fifth response pays, so divide the responses by the ratio.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies. Each reward needs five responses, so divide instead.
That subtracts the ratio once. Count how many sets of five fit in the total.

questions.prompt: On a fixed-interval 10-second schedule, a rat presses every 3 seconds for 60 seconds. The first press at least 10 s after the previous reward is rewarded. How many rewards does it earn?
hints: The first press at or after 10 s is at 12 s.
The next must come at least 10 s after 12 s.
Keep stepping until 60 s and count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rewarded presses fall at 12, 24, 36, 48 and 60 s: five rewards.

questions.onCorrect: Only presses can be rewarded, and presses fall every 3 seconds, so each reward lands a little after the interval.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the time by the interval. A reward needs a press, and presses come every 3 seconds.
That is the number of presses, not the number of rewards.
